content.title: Part spectacle, part family tradition: Pittsburgh’s St. Patrick’s Day Parade kicks off spirited celebration
content.text: The sound of bagpipes filled the morning air long before the St. Patrick’s Day Parade began Downtown on Saturday morning. Scores of people lined the length of Liberty Avenue waiting for the 10 a.m. start of the parade. Some sported green beards, others leprechaun costumes — and plenty of kilts exposed legs to the crisp but sunny weather. Near the front of the parade, John Manore, who had come down from Toledo, Ohio, stood smoking a Kentucky Cheroots cigar — the kind Clint Eastwood smoked in many of his films and that have been puffed since the Civil War. He stood with his fellow infantrymen, waiting their turn to step off. His group represented the Union Army’s 116th Pennsylvania Infantry, a volunteer regiment that was part of the Irish Brigade during the war. The men wore a sprig of green on their caps. Mike Kraus, the captain of the group, said it was a reference to the Battle of Fredericksburg, when Brigadier General Thomas Meagher ordered his men to wear sprigs of green boxwood to “remember Ireland.” Mr. Kraus, of Oakland, said he has marched in the parade for more than 45 years. He and his group wore period-accurate uniforms adorned with original, 150-year-old buttons. Mr. Kraus even carried a sword that he said belonged to a soldier in the Battle of Fredericksburg, Va., Capt. John Flynn. They were among the many early sights at the parade, which itself dates back to 1869 and has run nearly continuously since 1950. City police had a sizable number of officers posted along the parade route to watch for shenanigans, but public safety spokeswoman Emily Bourne said, “Everything went smoothly. There were no incidents of note.” Every year, the parade — one of the largest in the country — brings out an estimated 200,000 to 350,000 spectators, plus thousands of marchers, according to Visit Pittsburgh. This year’s edition featured more than 200 floats, marching units and bands. Corey O’Connor — who also says he has marched in the parade for decades — donned a bomber jacket with “Ancient Order of Hibernians” embroidered on the back for his first parade as Pittsburgh mayor. He tossed candy to kids waiting to pounce from the sidewalks. Groups representing high school marching bands, Irish dance schools and Irish fraternities also made their way down Liberty Avenue toward the Boulevard of the Allies, throwing beads, honking vehicle horns, dancing jigs and playing instruments. Wearing a crown and sash, Molly McKenna, of Mt. Lebanon, this year’s Miss Irish Smiling Eyes, rode in a horse-drawn carriage accompanied by her court maidens, Kennedy Aryn Elizabeth Kuntz, of Collier, and Sidney Ann Hoover, of South Fayette. The horses sported green glitter on their hooves. Castle Shannon’s green emergency response vehicles matched perfectly with the sea of emerald green and the occasional shock of a leprechaun’s orange facial hair. The Pirate Parrot, fittingly green-furred, zoomed past on an electric scooter. He wasn’t the only mascot that day: Julia O’Connell donned her Easter bunny outfit for the second year in a row and towed a wagon full of candy from Grandpa Joe’s in the Strip District behind her. A few years ago, she won the Easter ensemble on a bidding website. “I got obsessed, like, I have to have that bunny costume. And I won it,” Ms. O’Connell said. “And I’m like, OK — I have it. What do I do with it?” She asked her husband, Sean, the parade’s solicitor for more than 15 years, if she could wear it in the parade and he said “absolutely.” He’s a seasoned marcher. Mr. O’Connell has been participating in the parade since he was a kid, he said, back when he marched alongside his grandfather in the 1970s. His grandfather emigrated from Ireland in 1923 through Ellis Island before settling down in Hazelwood, he said. As the parade inched forward, bands banged drums that boomed beneath a railroad bridge beside Downtown’s Greyhound bus and Amtrak stations before entering the bright sunlight. Crowds decked out in shamrocks and beads high-fived parade participants, hugging mascots and diving for candy. Farther down Liberty Avenue beads hung from trees, and cherry blossoms just beginning to sprout added some pink to the mix. But it was the huge yellow vehicles that seemed to steal the show. As the machines passed, spectators turned to one another in awe, asking, “What is that?” They were a brigade of Pittsburgh International Airport’s snow blower, tow truck and firetruck, promoting Aer Lingus’ new flight directly from Pittsburgh to Dublin, Ireland. A young girl sat beside the driver of the snow blower, reveling in laying on the horn to a sea of cheers. Two flight attendants in uniform led the procession, and the audience burst into applause, some yelling, “That’s our flight!” All around, there were quirks and spectacles for every taste: a Tesla Cybertruck filled with people in green Care Bear suits, tossing out candy; dogs wearing kilts; Jeeps dressed as leprechauns — top hat on the roof with an orange beard hanging from the front grille; and Great Danes with green shamrocks painted onto their fur and one with a mini-saddle on its tall frame. Finley Sieber’s favorite part was the dogs, she said. Finley, 12, of Shaler, has been coming to the parade since she was born, her mother said. In fact, nearly everyone in the crowd around her was a family member — dozens of them. It was a Sieber tradition, family patriarch Mike Sieber, 66, said. He’s missed very few St. Patrick’s Day parades in the last six decades. For the past 39 years, the Sieber family has rented Downtown hotel rooms so that after the parade, the whole family could get together, put on a talent show and swim in the hotel pool. Finley and her cousin, Hadley Mares, 12, had a competition going for who could collect the most tossed beads. (Hadley was in the lead). Having seen the parade every year they’ve been alive, Finley and Hadley both said they plan on coming back to celebrate for years to come.
